div.div: IPVS still uses conntrack,but it uses it differently and much more efficiently than iptables mode does.

div.div: Security Groups for Pods (SGP) is an EKS feature that allows you to treat a Pod like a first-class AWS citizen. Instead of all Pods on a node sharing the same "security identity" (the node's Security Group), specific Pods can have their own firewall rules.

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: Standard EKS networking assigns secondary IPs from the node's ENI to Pods. SGP changes this to a Trunking model

div.div: The Trunk ENI: A special "master" network interface (aws-k8s-trunk-eni) attached to the EC2 node.

div.div: The Branch ENI: For every Pod that needs a custom Security Group, EKS creates a Branch ENI (aws-k8s-branch-eni).

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.div: The Connection: The Branch ENI is "plugged into" the Trunk ENI.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 228px; height: 1px; padding-top: 506px; margin-left: 1881px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: The Security: You apply the AWS Security Group directly to the Branch ENI. Since that ENI is dedicated to one Pod, that Pod now has its own unique virtual firewall.

div.div: Branch ENI is a physical-to-virtual mapping designed for isolation

div.div: Density: Using Branch ENIs reduces the number of "standard" Pods you can run on a node because the Trunk ENI takes up one of the instance's ENI slots.

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
When to avoid ENI Trunking:
You should stay in the "Normal Case" unless you have a specific compliance requirement (like PCI-DSS) that mandates using AWS-level firewalls instead of Kubernetes internal ones.
For most AI and web workloads, standard NetworkPolicies (using Calico or Cilium) are faster and don't reduce your pod density (they use eBPF or iptables).

box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: By default, Kubernetes Network Policies are like a "specification without an implementation." While you can write the YAML to block traffic, the basic AWS VPC CNI was originally designed only to handle routing (giving pods IPs and moving packets). It didn't actually "read" the security rules you wrote.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 238px; height: 1px; padding-top: 380px; margin-left: 1126px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: This is why you traditionally needed a 3rd-party Policy Engine like Calico or Cilium to act as the "Security Guard" sitting on top of the VPC CNI's "Roads."
